summary:
Lithuania is workable for a trans visitor but operates one of Europe's least functional legal-gender-recognition regimes. The Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to change legal gender through medical intervention, yet the implementing legislation has never been adopted. The Lithuanian Gay League counts the resulting gap as 18 years old; the public broadcaster counts 17. Both figures describe the same condition: a statutory right with no procedure behind it.

The courts declined to break the deadlock in 2025. In August the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case concerning the amendment of civil-status gender documents and referred to the Constitutional Court the question of whether the relevant provisions comply with the Constitution. In September the Constitutional Court declined to examine that request, leaving unaddressed the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.

The practical consequence for a visitor is straightforward. Lithuania has no route by which a trans person's documents can be brought into line with lived gender, so entry, border checks and any interaction with officials proceed on the identity data as issued abroad. No visa, entry or residence provisions specific to LGBT visitors are set out in Lithuanian law.

Public incitement to violence against LGBT people is expressly prohibited under Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code. A 2010 preliminary investigation found that 160 of roughly 180 recorded hate-speech instances, most of them online, concerned the LGBT community, with perpetrators usually fined and computers occasionally confiscated. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records a systemic lack of targeted support for LGBTI hate-crime victims, which means reporting a bias incident is likely to be a solitary process rather than a supported one.

Assembly is legally protected but has a history of obstruction and of inadequate policing. The Seimas Ombudsperson found in 2024 that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly at an LGL gathering, responding inadequately to hostile provocateurs, and recommended measures to secure effective assembly rights. Earlier Pride events were halted by courts, delayed through litigation and met with arrests and violence; participation has since grown to around 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and roughly 5,000 in 2023.

The expressive framework has loosened. On 18 December 2024 the Constitutional Court struck down the anti-LGBT provisions of the Law on the Protection of Minors as a violation of Article 25, freedom of speech, following an ECHR Grand Chamber ruling in January 2023 that the censorship of a children's book involving same-sex relationships breached Article 10. Earlier attempts to criminalise 'public propagation of homosexual relations' were rejected by the Seimas in 2011 and 2013.

Partnership recognition moved in April 2025. On 17 April the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions, including for same-sex couples, contradicts the Constitution, and allowed same-sex couples to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas adopts a comprehensive law. Marriage remains limited to opposite-sex couples under Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code.

Reporting in May 2025 documented trans people describing open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse at work, with experts describing systemic labour-market discrimination. Trans visitors who work locally or attend professional settings should expect that environment rather than a neutral one.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 also covers a four-year asylum process for LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon who were ultimately granted protection after enduring dire camp conditions, during which a psychologist was convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts. The prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule was complicated by his immunity as an MEP.

Legislative hostility has been persistent and only partly defeated. In September 2013 the Seimas considered five separate anti-gay and anti-trans bills, among them a statutory ban on gender reassignment grounded in the claim that gender is determined genetically at conception, a same-sex adoption ban, fines of up to €1,800 for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech. The companion 2013 bill on 'public propagation of homosexual relations' was rejected by Parliament, as an equivalent 2011 attempt had been.

The 2009 Law on the Protection of Minors, passed by 87-6 in an override of President Adamkus's veto and condemned by Amnesty International as a huge step backwards, was amended in December 2009 to replace the anti-LGBT clauses with a broader ban on information promoting conceptions of marriage or family other than those in the Constitution. That provision was used to restrict a 2013 Pride advertisement to night-time broadcast with an adult-content logo, and in 2014 the Ministry of Culture age-labelled and then banned a children's book whose two stories involved same-sex relationships, the censorship later ruled unlawful in Strasbourg.

Partnership reform has drawn sustained counter-mobilisation: a bill was preliminarily approved 46-17 in May 2017 and remained pending, and in May 2021 more than 10,000 people protested against partnership legislation in Vilnius. The January 2019 Constitutional Court ruling requiring residence permits for foreign same-sex spouses, following the European Court of Justice in Coman, shows the same pattern of judicial protection outrunning legislative action.
localsOnly:
The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson published 'The Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania' in 2024, the second national review after 2019, covering the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes. It records the absence of a legal framework and of any strategic approach to trans rights at state level.

Workplace treatment is documented in detail: trans people describe open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse, and experts describe labour-market discrimination as systemic rather than incidental.

Family law remains closed. Marriage is limited to opposite-sex couples by Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code, and adoption is unavailable to same-sex couples because marriage is a precondition; although single applicants are theoretically eligible, adoption by single gay people is not legally possible in practice. President Gitanas Nauseda stated in September 2021 that he would do his best to block adoption demands from Kaunas Pride organisers. Only 24 same-sex households were declared in the 2011 census.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal since 1993, two years after the end of Soviet occupation, after having been criminal during the interwar period and under Soviet rule. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 for EU accession and raised to 16 on 2 July 2010 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the outcome of the 2013 bill proposing a statutory ban on gender reassignment, so whether it was withdrawn, rejected or lapsed is unresolved here.

No source in the inventory records trans-specific assault, detention or border incidents with dates and outcomes, so the summary's violence assessment rests on the general hate-speech and assembly record rather than on trans-specific case data.

Nothing is sourced on whether Lithuanian border or consular screening asks questions capable of outing a trans traveller, beyond the absence of LGBT-specific entry rules; that gap is unresolved rather than confirmed as low-risk.

Healthcare access is documented as a barrier for residents in the 2024 national review, but no source addresses whether a short-term visitor could obtain gender-affirming medication or continuity of care in Lithuania.
